author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

text:
New "Skill Tree" for the AI Era:

​Level 1: 

Conditioning and Intent
​The "blank box" is a trap. Being technical now means mastering:

​Intent Specification: Writing ultra-tight problem contracts so the model can't hallucinate a path out.

​Context Engineering: Curating the exact data that enters the context window.
​Constraint Design: Using schemas and rubrics to turn a "slot machine" into a reliable machine.

​Level 2: Authority without Authorship

​You no longer need to write every line to own the outcome.

​Verification Design: Building automated mechanisms to ensure "truth."

​Chain of Custody: Ensuring every LLM claim has traceable evidence. If you can’t verify it, you don't own it.

​Level 3: Failure Mode Taxonomy

​Chatting is a hobby; workflows are a career.
​Real leverage comes from moving beyond the chat box into automated pipelines.

​You must develop a taxonomy for failure—knowing exactly why a system broke (was it a bad tool call, poor context, or model drift?).

​Level 4: The Eval Harness

​This is the ceiling for most AI implementations.
​To scale, you need Eval Harnesses—test sets that allow you to swap models or prompts without playing "Russian roulette" with your production environment.

​You stop hand-crafting "gears" and start building the factory.

---

If you’ve been feeling "behind" lately, it’s because the very definition of being technical has fundamentally shifted. We are moving from being craftsmen to being system architects. The goal isn't to work harder than the AI; it’s to provide the orchestration that makes the AI useful.

​Inspired by insights from Andrej Karpathy and the framework breakdown by Nate B. Jones.
